title: Agnostic direct-sum learning rates
formal: Does the single-instance agnostic learning rate determine all Cartesian-power learning rates up to constant factors? Precisely, for every two nonempty concept classes \(\mathcal C\subseteq Y^{X}\) and \(\mathcal D\subseteq Z^{W}\) on nonempty countable input and label sets, suppose there are \(a,b>0\) such that \[a\,e_{\mathcal D}(n)\le e_{\mathcal C}(n)\le b\,e_{\mathcal D}(n)\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge1.\] Must there then be \(a',b'>0\), allowed to depend on the two classes but not on \(n\) or \(r\), such that \[a'\,e_{\mathcal D^{r}}(n)\le e_{\mathcal C^{r}}(n)\le b'\,e_{\mathcal D^{r}}(n)\qquad\text{for every }n,r\ge1?\] This is the constant-factor rate-determination form of the source's agnostic Open Question 3. The countable-domain convention and constant-factor interpretation are explicit editorial choices; the source paper also asks separate realizable-learning and compression questions.
why: A direct-sum law would explain whether learning several tasks together has a statistical cost determined by the difficulty of one task. In the agnostic setting, whole-tuple loss and unrestricted correlations can make that question depend on class structure not visible in its ordinary learning rate.
status_note: Uncertain pending assessment of the matching claimed refutation in arXiv:2608.06951v1 (7 August 2026). progress.text: Hanneke, Moran and Waknine ask how the agnostic learning curve changes under Cartesian powers, separately from their realizable-learning, uniform-convergence and compression questions.

More, Das and Gupta post Theorem 1 claiming a negative rate-level answer. Its model and theorem statement match the selected formulation, but this review has not independently verified the proof or established a peer-reviewed resolution.

importance.reason: A general question about how agnostic learning difficulty scales across multiple tasks and whether a single-instance minimax rate contains enough information; the source’s distinct compression and realizable questions are not bundled into this target.
importance.basis: Saved question, title, and category scope; importance review only, not a fresh proof or open-status review.

sentences: The question asks whether comparable single-instance agnostic learning rates force comparable rates for every number of simultaneous tasks.
The learning curve is minimax expected excess zero-one error, with arbitrary distributions and improper deterministic learners.
For a Cartesian power, each example is a complete tuple and any wrong coordinate makes the tuple prediction incorrect.
The comparison constants must be independent of both sample size and number of tasks.
An August 2026 preprint claims a finite binary counterexample, so the card records an unresolved verification status for that claimed refutation.

definitions:
For a nonempty class \(\mathcal H\subseteq V^{U}\) on countable sets \(U,V\), and any probability distribution \(P\) on \(U\times V\), let \(L_P(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim P}[h(x)\ne y]\). Define \[e_{\mathcal H}(n)=\inf_{A_n}\sup_{P}\left(\mathbb E_{S\sim P^{n}}L_P(A_n(S))-\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}L_P(h)\right).\] Here \(A_n:(U\times V)^{n}\to V^{U}\) ranges over all deterministic learning rules and is chosen before \(P\); it may depend on \(\mathcal H\) and \(n\). It need not be computable, and may output a predictor outside \(\mathcal H\). The training sample consists of \(n\) independent pairs from \(P\). The outer expectation is over that sample; the risk uses a fresh independent pair. All countable sets have their discrete sigma-algebras. The countable sample space makes these expectations well-defined even when the hypothesis class is uncountable. Labels may have arbitrary noise. Infima are not assumed to be attained. The rate is a dimensionless minimax expected excess probability of error in \([0,1]\).

For \(r\ge1\), \(\mathcal H^{r}\) consists of all maps \((x_1,\ldots,x_r)\mapsto(h_1(x_1),\ldots,h_r(x_r))\) with \(h_1,\ldots,h_r\in\mathcal H\). Its input set is \(U^{r}\) and its label set is \(V^{r}\). Apply the same learning-curve definition to this class. Each of the \(n\) examples is now an entire input–label tuple. Its coordinates can be arbitrarily correlated: \(P\) ranges over every distribution on \(U^{r}\times V^{r}\), not just product distributions. A tuple prediction incurs loss one whenever any coordinate differs from the label tuple, and zero otherwise. This is whole-tuple zero-one loss, not a sum or average of coordinate losses. The learner for the product may also be improper, so its output need not act separately on each coordinate.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the rate-determination implication. A refutation must give two admissible classes with comparable single-instance curves but prove that no positive constants independent of both \(n\) and \(r\) compare their product curves. A positive answer must cover every such pair of classes and all positive sample sizes and product multiplicities. The target is a proposition about constant-factor rate information; it does not ask whether exact numerical single-instance curves encode additional information.

context_blocks.text: The inherited card contained the title of a paper posing several independent problems. This revision selects its agnostic rate question and makes the precision of the proposed relationship explicit. It does not assert that the other questions in that paper are equivalent or resolved.

The comparison is between expected error and the best predictor in the target class under the same distribution. Bounding the total error of separately learned coordinates does not automatically bound this excess error against the best whole-tuple predictor.

The order of quantifiers matters. Constants depending on the number of tasks would allow different behavior to be hidden as that number increases. This formulation requires a single pair of comparison constants for all sample sizes and multiplicities.

The August 2026 preprint claims a counterexample using \(X=Y=\{0,1\}\): one class contains the two constant functions, and the other contains the zero function and the identity function. It claims product rates respectively of order \(n^{-1/2}\) and \(\min\{1,\sqrt{r/n}\}\), while both single-instance rates are of order \(n^{-1/2}\). The claim concerns the exact whole-tuple, improper model used here, and would refute this implication.
